questions.prompt: Because HTTP is stateless, what must a web server do on every request?

options.text: Re-authenticate/authorize, since no memory of prior requests is guaranteed
Trust that a prior login still applies without checking
Store all state in the browser and trust it
Reopen the TCP connection for each byte

questions.explanation: HTTP keeps no memory between requests, so the server must re-verify identity and permission on each request (complete mediation).

questions.prompt: An 'origin' in the same-origin policy is the combination of scheme, host, and ____.
questions.explanation: An origin is scheme + host + port; the same-origin policy blocks script from one origin from reading another origin's data.

questions.prompt: Which are categories in the OWASP Top 10 (2021)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Broken Access Control (A01), Injection (A03), and SSRF (A10) are all OWASP Top 10 (2021) categories; 'Slow Wi-Fi' is not a security risk category.

questions.prompt: Match each HTTP status code to its meaning.
questions.explanation: 200 is success, 401 means not authenticated, 403 means authenticated but not authorized, and 500 is a server error.

questions.prompt: Order what the server should do at the trust boundary for a request.

items.text: Safely encode output back to the browser

questions.explanation: At the trust boundary the server authenticates, authorizes the specific object, validates input, uses safe APIs, and encodes output — never trusting the client.

questions.prompt: Why is client-side validation not a security control?

options.text: An attacker can bypass the browser entirely (e.g. with curl or a proxy)
It runs too slowly to be useful
Browsers encrypt it so the server can't read it

questions.explanation: Client-side checks are for usability; attackers send requests directly, bypassing the browser, so all security validation must happen on the server.
